Summary of Week 6 Lecture: Spatial Machine Learning & Advanced Regression ￼

⸻

1. Baseline Model Building
	•	Began with a simple linear regression predicting SalePrice from LivingArea (structural feature only).
	•	Coefficient: each extra sq ft adds ≈ $216.
	•	R² ≈ 0.13 → explains only 13% of variation.
	•	Missing factors: location, amenities, neighborhood quality, crime, schools.

⸻

2. Adding Predictors
	•	Adding number of bathrooms increased R² slightly (to 0.14).
	•	Demonstrated diminishing returns from structural-only models.
	•	Emphasized the need for spatial variables to capture “location, location, location.”

⸻

3. Introducing Spatial Data
	•	Converted tabular data to spatial (sf) format using coordinates.
	•	Transformed CRS from EPSG:4326 to MA State Plane for accurate distance measures.
	•	Joined parcels with neighborhood polygons using st_join().
	•	Visualized median prices by neighborhood, showing clear spatial clustering:
	•	Back Bay, Beacon Hill, South End highest.
	•	Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan lowest.

⸻

4. Regression with Categorical (Dummy) Variables
	•	Used neighborhood name (name) as a factor.
	•	R automatically creates dummy variables for each neighborhood.
	•	One neighborhood (Allston) becomes the reference category.
	•	Model interpretation:
	•	Positive coefficient → more expensive than Allston.
	•	Negative coefficient → cheaper than Allston.
	•	Example: identical houses differ by millions between Back Bay ($8.5M) and Roxbury ($0.33M).

⸻

5. Interaction Effects
	•	Question: does square footage matter equally in all areas?
	•	Built interaction models:
	•	Model 1 (no interaction): same slope everywhere.
	•	Model 2 (interaction): slope differs by neighborhood wealth.
	•	Defined “wealthy neighborhoods” = Back Bay, Beacon Hill, South End, Bay Village.
	•	Result:
	•	Wealthy areas have much steeper slopes (≈ $985/sq ft vs. $95 in others).
	•	Confirms Luxury Premium Hypothesis — larger homes in wealthy areas command disproportionate premiums.

⸻

6. Conceptual Takeaways
	•	Spatial features and fixed effects are critical to avoid biased estimates.
	•	Spatial autocorrelation violates OLS independence assumptions.
	•	Remedies: include location terms, fixed effects, or spatial regression models.
	•	Understanding geography improves both predictive accuracy and policy relevance in housing analytics.

⸻

Key Terms: baseline model, dummy variable, fixed effects, interaction term, spatial join, CRS transformation, hedonic model, Tobler’s First Law, spatial autocorrelation.
